subject: chemistry
title: Endothermic Reaction
summary: An endothermic reaction absorbs energy from its surroundings, usually as heat — like a cold pack getting cold, an egg cooking, or a plant using sunlight. It is the opposite of exothermic.

compareCandidate.label: Endothermic vs. exothermic
compareCandidate.description: An endothermic reaction ABSORBS energy — it cools its surroundings, like a cold pack or a cooking egg. An exothermic reaction RELEASES energy — it warms its surroundings, like a fire or hand warmer. One takes in, the other gives out.

parts: Needs an energy supply to run
processes: Pulling heat out of the surroundings
Feeding on sunlight or other energy
Driving cold packs, cooking, and photosynthesis
plainLanguageExplanation: An endothermic reaction is a chemical reaction that absorbs energy from its surroundings. The name means 'heat coming in' — endo (in) + therm (heat). When such a reaction runs, it sucks energy out of whatever surrounds it, usually as heat — which is why the surroundings get COLDER. The classic example is a cold pack: you crack the inner packet, a chemical reaction starts, and it absorbs heat so eagerly that the pack freezes cold. Cooking an egg is endothermic too — the egg absorbs heat from the pan to transform. And the most important endothermic reaction on Earth is photosynthesis: a plant absorbs energy from sunlight to build sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Why does this happen? In an endothermic reaction, the products hold MORE energy than the reactants. That extra energy does not appear by magic — it has to be pulled in from the surroundings. So the surroundings lose heat and cool down. Endothermic reactions are the quiet absorbers of chemistry — they take energy in and leave the world a little cooler.

whyItMatters: Endothermic reactions power some of the most important processes on Earth — photosynthesis feeds the planet, cold packs ease injuries, and cooking transforms food. Understanding them explains why some reactions make things cold, and why the biggest energy input on the planet comes through plants absorbing sunlight.
didYouKnow: Every plant leaf is running endothermic reactions all day — absorbing sunlight to build sugars. When you eat a salad, you are eating the products of billions of endothermic reactions.
compareReason: The endothermic and exothermic reactions are opposite energy partners — comparing absorbing with releasing makes the whole energy story of reactions crystal clear.
